title: Hank's Sex Tape

jokes.text: Hank tells the audience the sign says 'Applesauce,' then corrects himself: 'It says applause.'
jokes.setup: Hank is warming up the studio audience and points to a sign, claiming it says 'Applesauce.'
jokes.punchline: He laughs it off as a joke — it says 'applause.' The bit reveals Hank's desperate, performative warmup-comic energy.
jokes.explanation: A mild warmup-act joke that works mostly because it characterizes Hank as the kind of guy who does this unironically. The joke itself is weak, but the self-aware framing of him performing to a captive studio audience gives it a satirical edge. Not especially original or quotable.

jokes.text: Hank: 'The better you are, the better Larry is.' — Hank building up the audience but inadvertently admitting his own irrelevance.
jokes.setup: Hank is telling the audience they're a big part of the show and should be enthusiastic.
jokes.punchline: He frames it as 'the better you are, the better Larry is' — completely erasing himself from the equation, oblivious to the self-deprecation.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Hank's complete lack of self-awareness — he is literally hyping his boss while ostensibly warming up the crowd for himself. It's a small, efficient character joke that rewards attention. Rewatch bonus because the more you know Hank, the funnier his obliviousness is.

jokes.text: Larry's monologue joke: Connie Chung was fired because her sign-off line was 'I do you a long time, joe.'
jokes.setup: CBS fired Connie Chung from the evening news. Larry says they're fans of hers.
jokes.punchline: She insisted her sign-off be 'I do you a long time, joe' — a racist/sexual parody of the 'Me love you long time' trope.
jokes.explanation: A mid-90s late-night topical joke that plays on racial and sexual taboo. The structure is solid — sympathetic setup flipped into transgression — but the punchline leans on a dated racial stereotype, which limits its earned_vs_cheap score. It works as a snapshot of 1990s late-night comedy sensibilities, and the show uses Larry's self-satisfaction at his own joke as a second beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I so rarely laugh At my own stuff That I'm overjoyed that Something struck me funny.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I so rarely laugh at my own stuff that I'm overjoyed that something struck me funny.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just laughed at his own Connie Chung joke, breaking his usual composure.
jokes.punchline: He calls attention to it — making his own vanity and self-regard the joke, with the meta admission that he considers himself above his own material.
jokes.explanation: This is efficient character comedy. Larry's self-regard is the engine of his character arc and it comes through cleanly here — he's so pleased with himself for being pleased with himself. The meta layer (a late-night host commenting on his own comedy mid-monologue) is proto-Curb in its awkward honesty. Strong character integration score because only Larry Sanders could deliver this line without it seeming like a humble brag.

jokes.text: McDonald's opening a kosher restaurant in Israel will be 'the first McDonald's to have the new Never Happy Meal.'
jokes.setup: McDonald's is opening its first kosher restaurant in Israel.
jokes.punchline: 'It will also be the first McDonald's to have the new Never Happy Meal.' — a play on 'Happy Meal' and Jewish cultural stereotypes.
jokes.explanation: A tight, economic wordplay joke that lands cleanly. 'Never Happy Meal' is a genuinely good pun — it functions on two levels (the McDonald's menu item and a Jewish-cultural-pessimism stereotype). The structure is efficient: setup in one sentence, punchline in one phrase. Limited by the fact that it's a generic late-night ethnic joke that any host could tell.

jokes.text: Larry teases the follow-up to the 'Women Who Smoke' calendar before laughing and delaying the punchline.
jokes.setup: Author Thomas Booth has a calendar called 'Women Who Smoke' to dispel the myth that they're unattractive. Larry says this is a follow-up to his previous calendar...
jokes.punchline: After laughing and stalling: 'Chicks with One Eye.' — The extended pause and Larry breaking before the punchline is itself the comedy.
jokes.explanation: The joke itself ('Chicks with One Eye') is disposable, but the performance beat — Larry laughing before he delivers it, then commenting 'I think this is as funny as the Connie Chung joke' — is a meta piece of character comedy that works within the show's satirical frame. The structure includes a deliberate withholding that builds minimal but real anticipation.

jokes.explanation: This is the second beat of a running Larry-as-his-own-critic gag. Works as a callback to joke #4 and deepens the portrait of Larry's narcissistic self-assessment. The meta quality of a host grading his own monologue jokes mid-air is a distinctly Larry Sanders move. Good character integration.

jokes.explanation: A sharp backstage moment exposing the manufactured reality of a talk show — Larry's intense control over how he appears versus how he actually is. 'Hank was just scanning' is a perfect throwaway that humanizes both characters efficiently. Strong character integration for Larry's controlling paranoia.

jokes.text: Promo concept pitches: 'Big Larry, Little Hank puppet. Big comedy, no strings attached.' / 'Larry and Hank by the pool in bathing suits. Summer of fun.' / 'Larry and Hank soaring over the audience. High-flying comedy!'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie must choose a promo concept for the show.
jokes.punchline: Three increasingly ridiculous concepts are pitched with breathless taglines — 'High-flying comedy!' — each worse than the last. Larry asks 'Who writes this shit?' Answer: 'Network publicist.'
jokes.explanation: Classic showbiz satire — the gap between the network's cheerful mediocrity and the talent's contempt. The escalating absurdity of the concepts (puppet → pool → soaring) earns the 'Who writes this shit?' reaction. The 'Network publicist' punchline is perfectly deadpan. Efficient industry-insider comedy.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Why do I have to be the little puppet?'
jokes.setup: The first promo option is 'Big Larry, Little Hank puppet.'
jokes.punchline: Hank's objection is not 'I don't want to be a puppet' — it's that he objects specifically to being the *little* puppet. His ego is so fragile that the SIZE of the puppet is the insult.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. The entire Hank Kingsley character — his wounded dignity, his subordinate status, his inability to see the bigger indignity — is compressed into five words. Only Hank would accept the premise of BEING a puppet while quibbling about his relative size to Larry. One of the episode's best character jokes.

jokes.text: Hank's response to winning the orange growers spokesperson job: 'I'm just juiced!' — then immediately realizing the inadvertent pun.
jokes.setup: Irene tells Hank he's been chosen as spokesperson for Southern Orange Growers. Hank, overwhelmed, blurts 'I'm just juiced!'
jokes.punchline: Sid immediately points out it's a pun. Hank's accidental wordplay about being 'juiced' for an orange growers deal lands as both genuine enthusiasm and accidental marketing genius.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the accidental nature of the pun and Sid's gleeful over-crediting of it ('Is that a funny? Yes.'). Hank's earnest obliviousness makes the pun funnier than if he'd intended it. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Hank learns the competition for the spokesperson job was Sandy Duncan, and they feared the 'eye thing' would suggest orange juice caused vision loss.
jokes.setup: Hank asks who he beat out for the spokesperson job.
jokes.punchline: 'Sandy Duncan... they were afraid the eye thing would be because of the orange juice.' — The brand's concern wasn't about talent but about the optics of a one-eyed spokesperson for a vitamin C product.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny dark corporate logic — the brand cares only about the product association, not the disability itself. The joke takes a slightly uncomfortable premise (Sandy Duncan's eye) and subverts it with such specific absurd reasoning that it works. Well-structured, efficient, and has an unexpected element.

jokes.text: Sid defending Hank to Irene: 'He doesn't even eat smoked whitefish.' — in response to 'Do you smoke marijuana?'
jokes.setup: Irene asks Hank the due-diligence question: 'Do you smoke marijuana?'
jokes.punchline: Sid jumps in: 'He doesn't even eat smoked whitefish.' — the logic being that 'smoked' anything is disqualifying, a completely absurd non sequitur that reveals Sid as a man running on instinct.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. It works on multiple levels: Sid's illogical but confident logic ('smoked = bad'), the Jewish cultural specificity of whitefish making Sid's character vivid, the perfect deadpan economy, and the fact that it answers a direct question with something that has no bearing on it whatsoever. This is the kind of joke that sounds effortless but required someone to find the exact right word ('whitefish'). Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its unexpected sharpness.

jokes.text: Hank's self-description: 'I come here, I do my work, I go home. I read, uh, the bridges of...' [Sid whispers] 'Madison County.' — Hank doesn't know the title of the book he's referencing.
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to present himself as a simple, wholesome man to the orange growers by listing his humble activities.
jokes.punchline: He can't even name the sentimental bestseller he's using as his character witness — Sid has to whisper the title. The performance of wholesomeness collapses into its own incompetence.
jokes.explanation: Elegant characterization joke — Hank is desperately performing simple virtue while being too dim to pull it off, needing his own agent to feed him the punchline of his own character pitch. The pause before Sid's whisper is a beautiful beat. Strong character integration because only Hank is precisely this kind of pompous fraud who undermines himself mid-sentence.

jokes.explanation: A structurally clever joke — the wrong answer IS proof of the answer to the original question. The person who answers 'to get to the other side' proves by that response that they are, in fact, stoned. It's a neat logical loop delivered with complete naturalism. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: Lines heard from the sex tape playing in the background: 'I shall wash, but I shan't be clean.' / 'Pinky's got the tits, Butsey's got the ass.'
jokes.setup: Hank's sex tape is playing on the TV in his office while his coworkers watch.
jokes.punchline: The specific, bizarre things Hank apparently says during sex — 'I shall wash, but I shan't be clean' (archaic, literary?) and the nicknames 'Pinky' and 'Butsey' — suggest a man whose private sexual persona is as pompously theatrical as his public one.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. 'I shall wash, but I shan't be clean' is one of the funniest things a person could say during sex — archaic, melodramatic, mortified — and it maps perfectly onto Hank's pompous, self-dramatizing character. 'Pinky's got the tits, Butsey's got the ass' adds absurdist specificity (what ARE these nicknames?). These lines are so precisely calibrated to Hank Kingsley that they couldn't exist in any other show. High rewatch bonus and quotability. Among the episode's best moments.

jokes.explanation: The comedy has a double punch: first the cringe of a coworker stumbling into porn, and second the specific content — Hank is roleplaying a Larry Sanders power dynamic during sex. 'Larry Sanders thinks he's the boss' as a sex roleplay line is darkly funny character work suggesting Hank's resentment of Larry leaches into his intimate life.

The personification of Hank's genitalia as a character with opinions — specifically opinions about his boss's producer — is so specific and strange it becomes iconic. This is exceptional character integration: the joke wouldn't exist without Larry Sanders' specific world where Artie is a constant authority figure Hank resents. Justifiably scores 8+.

jokes.text: Sid's crisis management via Rob Lowe: 'Nobody remembers the Rob Lowe tapes.'
jokes.setup: Hank is panicking about the sex tape getting out. Sid tries to calm him by invoking the Rob Lowe sex tape scandal as a precedent.
jokes.punchline: Everyone immediately responds 'Rob Lowe? Rob Lowe. Rob Lowe. Rob Lowe!' — three repetitions showing that everyone ABSOLUTELY remembers Rob Lowe. Sid's reassurance is the worst possible example.
jokes.explanation: The structure here is excellent — Sid's reassurance ('Nobody remembers') is instantly demolished by everyone in the room reflexively naming Rob Lowe four times. The repetition of 'Rob Lowe' is the punchline, and it lands through escalation. Strong character integration for Sid as a bumbling agent whose advice actively makes things worse. This is proto-Curb in its logic.

jokes.text: Sid's defense of Hank's sex tape situation vs. Rob Lowe: 'Rob Lowe has a playboy image. Do you like that? Hank Kingsley — people think of Hank as just a meat and potatoes guy. A guy you can invite over for dinner. 'Hey, Hank, what are you doing tonight? You're busy? What are you doing?' / 'Well, I'm just fucking two women!'
jokes.setup: Sid is explaining why the tape is more damaging for Hank than for Rob Lowe — Hank has a family-friendly image.
jokes.punchline: Sid's warm, folksy imagined dinner conversation ('Hey Hank, what are you doing tonight?') escalates to Hank interrupting with the actual punchline of his private life: 'Well, I'm just fucking two women!' — a brutal collision of the public and private Hanks.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The structure is brilliant: Sid builds a cozy, wholesome imagined dialogue ('meat and potatoes,' dinner invitations) until it can't hold the real Hank any longer. The punchline — Hank's own voice crashing through Sid's fantasy with 'I'm just fucking two women' — is a perfect compression of the episode's entire comic premise. Strong character integration for both Sid (delusional agent) and Hank (image vs. reality). Justifiably scores high.

jokes.text: Artie to Phil: 'That tape you copied is crawling around town like a fucking ebola virus.' / Phil: 'I just sent it to a friend.' / Artie: 'And then sent it into the world like the fucking ebola virus.'
jokes.setup: Artie confronts Phil about copying the tape. Phil minimizes it as just sending it to one friend.
jokes.punchline: Artie repeats the ebola virus metaphor twice — once as a statement of fact, once in answer to Phil's defense — perfectly applying the metaphor to the mechanism of viral sharing (before 'viral' was a common word). The repetition escalates the indictment.
jokes.explanation: The ebola metaphor applied to information spreading through social networks in 1995 is genuinely prescient comedy. Artie using 'fucking ebola virus' twice — the second time answering Phil's defense — shows the show understanding the mechanics of how content spreads virally, years before the concept existed. Strong Artie character voice. Justifiably scores high.

The juxtaposition of 'underground railroad' (heroic, historical, solemn) with 'of perverts' (deflating, specific, perfectly accurate) is a genuine piece of comedic craft. It's Artie's voice — world-weary, acerbic, deploying cultural references with precision. Highly quotable, pure economy. Justifiably scores 8+.

'I hope to hell we don't have to fire your ass' without any anger is more menacing than rage. Excellent character integration.

jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — six words ('I'm drunk. Actually my life is shit.') against Winkler's well-meaning cheerfulness. The brutality of the honesty in a context that calls for small talk is the joke. Strong character integration: Hank's fragile dignity cracking into unfiltered misery. The 'I'm drunk' as preamble/explanation is a particularly good touch.

jokes.setup: Henry Winkler appears to have heard about the sex tape and refers to it euphemistically as an 'exercise tape.'
jokes.punchline: Hank's indignant 'What are you, trying to be funny?' — directed at the Fonz — is both the cringe of a man whose embarrassment is now public knowledge and a comedy about someone not being able to take a joke.
jokes.explanation: A solid exchange. Winkler's 'exercise tape' euphemism is cheeky and the irony is clear. Hank's defensive reaction is good character work. The comedy of the Fonz ribbing Hank while Hank can't handle it is situationally funny.

jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed character comedy. The emotional sincerity of Hank's friendship speech is obliterated by a sex-tape-induced physical paranoia — 'Is my fly down?' mid-declaration of loyalty. It encapsulates Hank in one beat: the gap between the dignity he wants and the humiliation he inhabits. Great structure (buildup/deflation) and strong character integration. Justifiably scores 8+.

jokes.explanation: Larry's tag is perfectly timed and economical — 'To quote our president' repurposes Hank's defensive speech as a Clinton joke without being heavy-handed. The '2 or more' in Hank's original line is the setup, Larry's tag is the payoff. Strong structure: Hank walks into the joke without knowing it, Larry lands it without ceremony. The chemistry it produces ('There's our chemistry!') is an additional meta beat.

'All the way to Seinfeld' transforms a crass moment into a commentary on the show's competitive anxiety. The Menendez Brothers reference (the trial was ongoing at the time) gives Hank's murderous rage a specific cultural frame — and the 'take out daddy' tag implies Hank views Larry as a father figure he wants to kill, which is psychologically acute character work. The specificity of 'I'm Lyle, you're Eric' makes it funnier and darker. Strong character integration: only Hank would frame a murder fantasy through a celebrity trial. Justifiably scores high.

jokes.explanation: The polite inquiry 'Is this a bad time?' over obvious chaos is a classic structure — the understatement against the reality. Well-executed, strong economy. The specificity of the insults ('bald piece of shit,' 'fat little whore') in Hank's self-directed rage adds texture.

jokes.text: Irene Goodman from the orange growers walks in on Hank mid-brawl. Larry covers: 'He's just in the middle of practicing the sketch moves for the Ike Turner sketch we're doing later on the show.'
jokes.setup: The orange growers' spokesperson arrives while Hank is physically fighting a crew member.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately covers by attributing the violent brawl to rehearsal for an 'Ike Turner sketch' — domesticating workplace violence as performance, and also making a dark joke about Ike Turner's documented abuse of Tina Turner.
jokes.explanation: Larry's fast-thinking cover story is brilliant character comedy — he's so practiced at managing catastrophe that he improvises 'the Ike Turner sketch' without missing a beat. The Ike Turner reference normalizes the violence while simultaneously acknowledging it ('sketch moves'), and Irene's delighted 'Ike...[laughing]' suggests she either believes it or chooses to. Strong character integration for Larry's performative crisis management. High rewatch for the speed of the improvisation.

jokes.text: Larry showing Irene to his office, cascading into a defense of his awards: 'Don't touch anything, especially the awards. Keep your hands off them. There's a lot of them. Pen and pencil set, that's an award.'
jokes.setup: Larry is graciously offering his office to the orange growers rep but immediately issues possessive instructions.
jokes.punchline: The escalating defensiveness about his awards, culminating in 'pen and pencil set, that's an award' — Larry insisting on the value of what might be a promotional item.
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry Sanders character comedy — his insecurity expressed through proprietorial obsession with his awards. 'Pen and pencil set, that's an award' is the perfect detail: defending the dignity of what sounds like a participation trophy. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Phil reports only one tape remains — but it's at Hard Copy.
jokes.setup: Artie asks Phil how many tapes are out there. Phil says one.
jokes.punchline: 'But it's at Hard Copy.' — The worst possible destination for a sex tape in 1995, as Hard Copy was the premiere tabloid TV show. Artie's 'What?!' captures the horror perfectly.
jokes.explanation: The escalation works through specificity — not just 'a TV show' but 'Hard Copy,' the exact right tabloid entity for 1995. The pause between 'one' and 'but it's at Hard Copy' is a well-structured beat. Period-specific but effective.

jokes.text: Hank prays in his dressing room, confessing 'I'm not a religious man, I don't have a moral code to live by,' then quotes the orange growers contract verbatim as his prayer to God.
jokes.setup: Hank is alone, desperate, and drops to his knees in prayer.
jokes.punchline: His prayer is literally the boilerplate language from the orange growers spokesperson contract: 'maintain a public image consistent with the family values of the client's product... I will avoid any actions or appearance of actions detrimental to the same.' He's bargaining with God using legal language.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best single comedic moment. The joke works on every level: Hank has been so thoroughly colonized by the logic of commercial television that even his prayer is expressed in contract language. 'I will maintain a public image consistent with the family values of the client's product' is genuinely his idea of a vow to God. The spiritual deflation is complete and devastating. It's also beautifully earned — the whole episode has set up the orange growers deal. Exceptional character integration: this joke could only exist in Larry Sanders, and only be about Hank. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it.

jokes.text: Artie reveals he recovered the tape by calling 'my old service buddy Sumner Redstone.'
jokes.setup: Artie presents Hank with the last tape — he's managed to get it back from Hard Copy.
jokes.punchline: 'I had to pull some strings with my old service buddy Sumner Redstone' — Viacom/CBS chairman Sumner Redstone as an old army buddy of Artie's, implied to be in Artie's extensive Rolodex of powerful favors.
jokes.explanation: The implication that Artie — the weathered, profane TV producer — has a war-buddy relationship with the chairman of Viacom who controls Hard Copy is a perfect showbiz power fantasy. It also characterizes Artie as a man of old Hollywood connection who solves problems through personal networks rather than money. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Artie: 'The genie's back in the bottle.' / 'You're looking at a newborn Hank Kingsley. He's decent, and he's moral.' / Hank: 'Amen, brother.'
jokes.setup: The crisis has been averted. Artie pronounces Hank morally renewed.
jokes.punchline: The extreme solemnity of 'a newborn Hank Kingsley — he's decent, and he's moral' followed by Hank's earnest 'Amen, brother' — a man whose sex tape featured the phrase 'Up periscope' declaring himself reborn.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the tape arc with good irony — Hank's moral rebirth is as performative and hollow as everything else about him. 'Amen, brother' is the exact right level of self-delusion. Works as a closing beat for the tape storyline.

jokes.text: Larry's monologue: 'Full House was finally canceled.' [audience applause] 'Oh don't worry. Bob Saget's still doing the show where people get hurt.'
jokes.setup: Larry announces Full House has been canceled to audience applause.
jokes.punchline: Reassuring them that Bob Saget continues on America's Funniest Home Videos — 'the show where people get hurt' — a cutting description of AFV that implies Saget's nice-guy image is a mask for enjoying people's suffering.
jokes.explanation: A clean, economical showbiz joke. 'The show where people get hurt' is a genuinely sharp reduction of America's Funniest Home Videos, suggesting Saget's real talent is presiding over others' misfortune. The audience applause at Full House's cancellation adds the topical reality. Good structure.

jokes.text: The tape's final revelation: an additional tape has the Gilligan's Island roleplay in full — 'And who's the boss? Both women: You are!' / Hank chuckles nervously / 'Well, I just blew out the candles.' / 'You certainly did.' / 'Is that chemistry?'
jokes.setup: One more tape plays — after the apparent resolution of the crisis.
jokes.punchline: The Gilligan's Island roleplay continues — 'Who's the boss? You are!' — and Hank frames blowing out birthday cake candles as romantic/sexual ('I just blew out the candles. You certainly did.'). Then: 'Is that chemistry?' — an insane echo of his speech to Larry about on-screen chemistry.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful callback convergence: Hank's obsession with 'chemistry' (his word for the on-air bond with Larry that validates his existence) resurfaces in the most inappropriate context. 'Is that chemistry?' on a sex tape — asked after 'blowing out the candles' — completes Hank's character portrait: even in private, he's performing for an imagined audience and seeking validation. Excellent character integration and a structurally satisfying callback.

jokes.text: Hank alone on screen: 'I want this job. I want it. It means everything to me. So... just give me another chance. Please. Is there anything I can do? Anything!'
jokes.setup: Hank is apparently in front of the orange growers rep, having now lost or nearly lost the spokesperson deal.
jokes.punchline: The desperate, naked pleading — 'Is there anything I can do? Anything!' — both pathetic and a clear double-entendre given the tape context.
jokes.explanation: The 'Is there anything I can do? Anything!' is a loaded line given the episode — Hank, having just prayed with contract language, now makes a more human appeal that still sounds like it could offer inappropriate arrangements. The cringe is complete.

jokes.text: Irene Goodman responds to Hank's 'Is there anything I can do? Anything!' by whispering: 'Would you like to come up to my hotel tonight?'
jokes.setup: Hank has just made a desperate, open-ended offer — 'Is there anything I can do? Anything!' — to save his spokesperson deal.
jokes.punchline: The wholesome orange growers rep who's been conducting due diligence asks Hank to come to her hotel room. The buttoned-up corporate client is as morally complex as Hank — the tape scandal doesn't disqualify him, it attracts her.
jokes.explanation: A superb structural reversal. The entire episode has been about the orange growers deal being imperiled by Hank's sex tape — the conservative citrus brand as a symbol of family values. The reveal that the rep wants Hank in her hotel room demolishes that moral framework while also completing Hank's arc: his sex tape is simultaneously his professional downfall AND his personal calling card. Excellent misdirection and earned payoff. Justifiably scores 8+.

jokes.text: Hank's local affiliate promo: 'For only southern oranges have— Yee-haw! The taste of Dixie in a purty little carton.'
jokes.setup: Hank delivers a promo for Southern Orange Growers on set.
jokes.punchline: The promo is aggressively cornball — 'Yee-haw! The taste of Dixie in a purty little carton!' — delivered by a man who was just begging for redemption, and whose 'meat and potatoes' wholesomeness was exposed as a complete fiction.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the gap between who Hank actually is and the 'purty little carton' version he's selling. Coming after the hotel room invitation, it's a complete moral inversion played for deadpan irony. 'Yee-haw!' from Jeffrey Tambor is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Larry watches the commercial and asks: 'Hey! What do you think? Good, I wish it was me. Who'd you have to fuck to get this?'
jokes.setup: Larry watches Hank's finished commercial — it's clearly good
jokes.punchline: 'Who'd you have to fuck to get this?' — the Hollywood cliché applied perfectly, with the audience knowing the answer is literally 'Irene Goodman, Southern Orange Growers'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best closing line — a genuinely earned punchline that works on every level. 'Who'd you have to fuck to get this?' is an old Hollywood cliché, but here the audience KNOWS the answer. The cliché becomes literal, which transforms it from a tired expression into a devastating joke. The structure is perfect: the episode has spent twenty minutes setting up this exact question, and asking it casually in the final seconds is the ideal button. This is what 'earned' comedy means — the punchline is only this funny because of everything that preceded it.

jokes.text: Final line — Larry or Artie to Hank after the promo: 'Good. I wish it was me. Who'd you have to fuck to get this?'
jokes.setup: Hank has completed the orange growers promo and is presumably celebrating.
jokes.punchline: 'Who'd you have to fuck to get this?' — The Hollywood cliché of sexual quid pro quo as a closing line, which given Irene's hotel room invitation is not actually a joke but a precise description of events. The audience knows; the speaker may not.
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing line — a showbiz cliché that is simultaneously the most accurate description of what happened. 'Who'd you have to fuck to get this?' is played as a casual congratulatory joke, but the audience knows it's literally true. The double meaning doesn't need to be announced; it lands in the gap. Excellent structure (the irony is earned by the full episode), great economy, and a satisfying close. Justifiably scores high.
